outputs.L1:
Here is the text restored with its proper poetic lineation and punctuation. Since this is Charles Hamilton Sorley's well-known poem *"All the Hills and Vales Along,"* I have preserved every word and all original content, correcting only the formatting (line breaks, spacing, and punctuation) that had been lost:

---

**All the Hills and Vales Along**

All the hills and vales along
Earth is bursting into song,
And the singers are the chaps
Who are going to die perhaps.
O sing, marching men,
Till the valleys ring again.
Give your gladness to earth's keeping,
So be glad, when you are sleeping.

Cast away regret and rue,
Think what you are marching to.
Little live, great pass.
Jesus Christ and Barabbas
Were found the same day.
This died, that went his way.
So sing with joyful breath,
For why, you are going to death.
Teeming earth will surely store
All the gladness that you pour.

Earth that never doubts nor fears,
Earth that knows of death, not tears,
Earth that bore with joyful ease
Hemlock for Socrates,
Earth that blossomed and was glad
'Neath the cross that Christ had,
Shall rejoice and blossom too
When the bullet reaches you.
Wherefore, men marching
On the road to death, sing!
Pour your gladness on earth's head,
So be merry, so be dead.

From the hills and valleys earth
Shouts back the sound of mirth,
Tramp of feet and lilt of song
Ringing all the road along.
All the music of their going,
Ringing, swinging, glad song-throwing,
Earth will echo still, when foot
Lies numb and voice is mute.
On, marching men, on
To the gates of death with song.
Sow your gladness for earth's reaping,
So you may be glad, though sleeping.
Strew your gladness on earth's bed,
So be merry, so be dead.

---

outputs.L2:
Here is a paraphrased version that preserves the original meaning while using different language and phrasing:

---

Every hillside and every valley
Now erupts with melody,
And those who lend their voices
Are the soldiers who may soon perish.

Sing on, you marching soldiers,
Until the valleys echo once more.
Offer your joy as a gift to the earth,
So that even in death, you may be at peace.

Set aside your sorrow and regret,
Consider instead your destination.
The humble live briefly, the noble ones depart.
Christ and Barabbas alike
Faced judgment on the same day—
One perished, the other continued living.

So let your voices ring with happiness,
For death awaits you all the same.
The generous earth will surely gather
Every ounce of joy you offer it.

This is an earth immune to doubt or dread,
Familiar with mortality, untouched by sorrow.
This same earth once welcomed, without complaint,
The poison that ended Socrates' life.
This earth flourished and rejoiced
Beneath the cross where Christ once hung.
It will bloom and celebrate again
The instant a bullet finds you.

So march on, soldiers,
Down death's road, singing still!
Pour out your happiness upon the earth,
Find contentment even as you fall.

From every hill and every hollow,
The earth answers back with laughter—
The rhythm of footsteps, the rise of song
Echoing along the entire path.

All the melody of their marching,
Resounding, soaring, casting joy outward,
Will still echo in the earth
Even after feet grow still and voices fade.

Continue onward, singing soldiers,
Straight to death's threshold, still singing.
Plant your happiness for the earth to harvest,
That you might find peace, even in sleep.
Scatter your joy across the earth's resting place,
So you may be content, even as you die.

# The Paradox of Joy in the Face of Death: An Exploration of War Poetry's Central Theme

War poetry often grapples with humanity's most profound contradictions, and few themes capture this tension as powerfully as the image of soldiers marching toward their doom while singing with genuine joy. This striking juxtaposition forms the emotional and philosophical core of poetry that seeks to reconcile mortality with meaning, creating a complex meditation on how humans confront their own ending.

## Singing Toward Death

The central image that anchors this poetic vision is deeply unsettling in its beauty: young men marching to war, fully aware that death awaits many of them, yet filling the air with song rather than lamentation. This is not portrayed as naive ignorance of their fate, but rather as a conscious, almost defiant choice to embrace joy even as they walk toward near-certain destruction. The soldiers become symbols of a particular kind of courage—not the courage that denies fear, but the courage that transforms fear into celebration.

## A Call to Abandon Sorrow

The poem does not merely observe this phenomenon; it actively exhorts its subjects—and by extension, its readers—to release their grip on regret and sorrow. There is an urgent, almost imperative quality to this call, suggesting that dwelling in grief or dwelling on what might have been serves no purpose when facing an unchangeable destiny. Instead, the poem advocates for a radical acceptance that manifests as gladness, positioning joy not as denial but as the most dignified response to mortality's inevitability.

## The Indifferent Eternity of Earth

Central to the poem's philosophical framework is its portrayal of the Earth itself as an ancient, unfeeling witness to human mortality. The poem draws a direct line through history, invoking figures like Socrates and Christ—individuals whose deaths represent pivotal moments in human philosophical and spiritual consciousness—to demonstrate that death is neither new nor unique to these soldiers. The Earth has absorbed countless deaths across millennia, and yet it continues its eternal cycle, blooming season after season with complete indifference to human suffering or triumph. This is not portrayed as cruelty, but as a kind of cosmic constant—a reminder that individual mortality exists within a much larger, continuing pattern of life and renewal.

## The Eternal Echo

Yet within this seemingly bleak cosmic indifference, the poem finds a source of transcendence. The songs and joy expressed by the soldiers, though their voices will inevitably be silenced by death, do not simply vanish into nothingness. Instead, the poem suggests these expressions of joy become absorbed into the Earth itself, creating an eternal echo that persists beyond the individual lives that created it. This transforms the soldiers' songs from temporary human expression into something that joins the eternal fabric of existence—their joy becomes part of the same continuous pattern that has absorbed all human death and celebration throughout history.

## The Central Paradox

This philosophical tension crystallizes in the poem's haunting refrain: "so be merry, so be dead." This phrase encapsulates the entire paradox at the heart of the work—the simultaneous embrace of life's joy and death's certainty. Rather than presenting these as contradictory states, the refrain suggests they are intimately linked, perhaps even necessary companions. To be merry becomes a way of properly meeting death; to be dead becomes not an ending but a continuation of the joy that preceded it, absorbed into the eternal earth that outlasts all individual human experience.

Through this intricate weaving of imagery and philosophy, the poem constructs a vision of mortality that neither denies death's finality nor surrenders to despair. Instead, it offers a third path: finding authentic meaning and even celebration precisely at the moment when meaning might seem most threatened, suggesting that how we face our ending may matter as much as the ending itself.

# Expanding the Summary: A Poem of Soldiers Marching to War

## The Poetic Address

The poem takes the form of a direct address to soldiers who march toward what is likely their death in battle. Rather than adopting the expected tone of lamentation or somber warning, the speaker calls upon these men to sing—not with the false cheer of denial, but with a profound and paradoxical joy that acknowledges the gravity of their fate while transforming it into something meaningful. This is the central poetic device at work: the transmutation of potential tragedy into an act of defiant celebration.

## Earth as Eternal Witness

Central to the poem's power is its personification of the earth itself as a silent, ancient witness to human experience. The earth is figured not as an indifferent or passive backdrop to human suffering, but as a living repository that has absorbed countless moments of both triumph and sacrifice throughout the long span of history. Every song of joy, every act of courage, every death given in service of a cause greater than oneself—all of this becomes part of the earth's deep memory. The ground upon which soldiers march has heard laughter and lament alike; it has felt the weight of armies through the centuries, and it will continue to hold these echoes long after the immediate participants have passed into history.

## Historical and Spiritual Parallels

To reinforce this theme, the poem invokes two of history's most resonant examples of chosen sacrifice: Socrates and Christ. Both figures faced death not with terror but with a kind of transcendent acceptance—Socrates calmly drinking the hemlock in service of his philosophical convictions, and Christ accepting crucifixion as part of a larger spiritual purpose. By drawing these parallels, the poem elevates the soldiers' potential deaths from mere casualties of war into something aligned with humanity's greatest traditions of meaningful sacrifice. These figures serve as proof that death, when embraced with purpose and dignity, need not be purely tragic.

## The Paradox at the Poem's Heart

The true significance of this poem lies in its audacious reframing of death in battle. Where one might expect solemnity, fear, or grief, the poem instead insists upon gladness—not a naive or foolish gladness, but one that comes from understanding one's place within a larger continuum of human experience and sacrifice. This is the poem's central paradox: that facing likely death can become an occasion for joy rather than despair, precisely because that joy will itself become part of the eternal record that the earth keeps.

## Lasting Resonance

In its final effect, the poem suggests that the soldiers' song—their gladness in the face of mortality—will outlast their individual lives. Their joy will become absorbed into the earth alongside all the other moments of courage and sacrifice that have come before, joining the echoes of Socrates' calm philosophical resolve and Christ's redemptive suffering. Though the soldiers themselves may perish, the quality of their spirit, their choice to sing rather than despair, will resonate through time itself, becoming part of the same eternal witness that has recorded all human courage throughout history. In this way, the poem offers not comfort through denial of death, but transformation through the meaning that can be made of it.

# All, And, Till

There's a peculiar poetry in small words—the ones we skip over in reading, taking for granted, yet without which language would collapse into fragments. Consider three such words: *all*, *and*, *till*.

**All** suggests totality, the boundary of everything within a category. When we say "all is well," we make a claim about completeness, about nothing being left out. It's a word of ambition, reaching for the whole rather than settling for parts. Philosophers have wrestled with its implications—does "all" ever truly capture everything, or does it always leave some exception lurking at the edges? Yet in everyday speech, we use it freely, confidently, as though totality were simple to grasp.

**And** is the great connector, the word that builds sentences into chains, ideas into sequences. It asks for nothing in return except continuation. "This and that," "now and then," "again and again"—and keeps things moving forward, refusing to let a thought end when another might follow. There's something democratic about it too; and doesn't rank what it joins, doesn't say one thing matters more than another. It simply adds, accumulates, extends.

**Till** speaks of patience and duration, of waiting for something to arrive. "Till death do us part," "wait till morning," "not till you're ready"—till marks the space between now and some awaited moment. It's temporal, forward-looking, but also bounded; it implies an endpoint even as it describes the stretch of time before that point.

Together, these three words—all, and, till—trace a quiet arc: totality, connection, endurance. They remind us that meaning often lives not in the grand vocabulary of complex ideas, but in the small, humble words that hold sentences—and thoughts—together.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a World War I poem about soldiers marching cheerfully toward their deaths, using nature and earth imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Sowing**

They went like larks let loose from winter's fist,
boots drumming rhythms on the chalky lane,
their laughter rising thick as morning mist
above the hedgerows silvered after rain.

Young wheat stood green and eager in the field,
not knowing yet the scythe that names it grain—
so too these boys, their gladness unconcealed,
marched toward the harvest of another plain.

The poppies hadn't bloomed yet, but they would,
red as the cheeks of boys who sang off-key,
who tossed their caps like seeds into the wood
and could not see what red seeds come to be.

Oak trees lined the road in stately rows,
old sentinels who'd watched such marching men
for generations—watched how spring bestows
its green on those who won't see spring again.

The earth received them as she does all things:
the fallen leaf, the frost, the plow, the bone.
She has no grief for what the season brings.
She only knows the growing, not alone

but layered—death on death, a loam of years,
where boys who marched with mud upon their boots
become the soil that feeds the wheat, that hears
no singing now, only the deepening roots.

They went like larks. The larks came home that year.
The fields grew gold again, indifferent, true.
And somewhere, still, if you bend down to hear,
the earth remembers what the living knew.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of a WWI soldier's marching song, blending themes of death, joy, and sacrifice, referencing Christ and Socrates.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Marching Song of the Willing Dead**

*(Sung to a jaunty tune, boots striking mud in time)*

We're marching down to glory, boys,
with mud up to our knees,
We've traded in our Sunday joys
for lice and bayonets and fleas—
But sing! Oh sing the chorus loud,
let no man's voice be still,
For we are young and we are proud
and marching up the hill!

*Chorus:*
Oh it's hey and ho and away we go,
with a laugh to spend the pain,
For Christ hung high on a wooden tree
and we'll not grumble at the rain!
Socrates supped his cup with cheer,
and reasoned till the end—
So lift your voice, there's naught to fear,
we're marching round the bend!

The chaplain reads of Calvary,
of nails and vinegar wine,
He says our Lord bled willingly
so we should like bleed fine—
And Socrates, that ugly Greek,
he drank his hemlock down,
He didn't wail, he didn't shriek,
he wore no soldier's frown.

*Chorus:*
Oh it's hey and ho and away we go,
past the wire and the wreck,
For a man can die with his head held high
though the shrapnel breaks his neck!
The prophets died, the sages too,
for truths they'd not deny—
So we'll go singing, me and you,
we've company on high!

Tommy's lost his leg, poor lad,
but he's laughing fit to burst,
Says the pain's not half so bad
as the thirst, boys, as the thirst!
We'll drink our tea from a rusted tin,
we'll toast the King and Fate,
And when the whistle calls us in
we'll go before it's late.

*Chorus:*
Oh it's hey and ho, the bugles blow,
the dawn is stained with red,
But joy's a thing that shells can't kill
though they've numbered us with the dead.
For Christ knew death and Socrates knew,
and neither turned to flee—
So husband your fear, there's nothing new
in this old crossed-the-Rubicon spree!

When the guns fall still and the smoke has cleared
and they count what's no longer there,
Let them say we sang as the night drew near,
let them say we didn't care—
Not for the pain, nor the mud, nor the cost,
we gave what we had to give,
And whether it's Heaven or all is lost,
we sang while we tried to live.

*Final Chorus:*
So it's hey and ho and away we go,
with a song for the wooden cross,
For a cup of hemlock or a crown of thorns
teaches a man his loss
Is nothing at all if he goes out singing,
his laughter a kind of prayer—
So march, boys, march, let the bells be ringing,
we're already halfway there.
